analysis.one_liner: Orders safety testing standards for the lithium-ion batteries that power e-bikes and scooters.
analysis.headline: A bipartisan battery-safety bill cleared a Senate committee but died without a floor vote when the 118th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have required the Consumer Product Safety Commission to write a mandatory national safety standard for the rechargeable lithium-ion batteries used in e-bikes, e-scooters, and similar devices, aimed at preventing battery fires. It was introduced by Senator Gillibrand with cosponsors from both parties, was approved by the Senate Commerce Committee, and was placed on the Senate calendar in December 2024 — but the full Senate never voted on it before the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Everyone who rides, stores, or lives near e-bikes and e-scooters — including delivery workers who rely on them for a living and tenants in dense apartment buildings where battery fires spread fastest. A mandatory federal standard would bar the least safe batteries from the market.
analysis.who_benefits_short: E-bike riders, delivery workers, apartment residents

how_it_helps.text: Requires the CPSC to issue a final consumer product safety standard within 180 days of enactment for rechargeable lithium-ion batteries used in micromobility devices, including e-bikes and e-scooters, to protect against fire risk [S2] [S3].
Lets the CPSC decide which battery types and device types fall within the standard's scope, based on what is reasonably necessary to protect against fires [S3].
Treats the new standard as a rule under section 9 of the Consumer Product Safety Act, giving it the full enforcement machinery of a mandatory product safety rule [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Manufacturers and importers of e-bikes, e-scooters, and their batteries, who would bear the cost of testing and certification — costs that could be passed to consumers as somewhat higher prices. Sellers of the cheapest, uncertified batteries could be pushed out of the market.
analysis.who_pays_short: Battery and micromobility manufacturers and importers

drawbacks.text: Compliance with a mandatory safety standard would add testing and certification costs for makers and importers, and some of that cost would likely show up in the price of e-bikes and scooters [S3].
The bill set a tight 180-day deadline for the CPSC to finish the standard, which critics could reasonably argue is too little time for careful rulemaking on a technical product [S3].
To the extent uncertified batteries cost less, removing them from the market could pinch low-income riders and delivery workers who depend on the cheapest available equipment [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits outweigh the costs. Lithium-ion battery fires in e-bikes and scooters have caused deaths, injuries, and building fires, especially in dense cities where delivery workers keep bikes in apartments and hallways. The cost of the bill is modest testing and certification expense for manufacturers — the kind of cost a well-designed standard routinely imposes to keep dangerous products off the market. The main design criticism is the short rulemaking deadline, not the goal.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate Commerce Committee approved the bill and put it on the Senate's calendar in December 2024, but the full Senate never voted on it before the Congress ended in January 2025, so it died.

narrative.text: Senator Gillibrand introduced the bill on March 28, 2023, with cosponsors from both parties, and it was referred to the Senate Commerce Committee [S1] [S5].
On July 31, 2024, the committee ordered the bill to be reported favorably without amendment [S5].
On December 17, 2024, Chair Cantwell reported the bill to the Senate without amendment, and it was placed on the Senate Legislative Calendar under General Orders as Calendar No. 718 [S5].
No further action followed: the bill never received a floor vote, and the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025, killing the bill [S5] [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Manufacturers and importers of uncertified, cheaper lithium-ion batteries are better off: no mandatory federal standard was ever imposed, so the least safe batteries could keep being sold, and consumers remain exposed to the fire risk the bill targeted.

for.name: Sen. Kirsten Gillibrand
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill requiring a CPSC safety standard for lithium-ion batteries in micromobility devices.

for.name: Sen. Charles Schumer, Sen. Marsha Blackburn, Sen. Mike Braun, and Sen. Jon Tester
for.role: Original cosponsors (2 Senate Democrats, 2 Senate Republicans)
for.what_they_did: Signed on as the bill's four cosponsors, giving it bipartisan sponsorship.

for.name: Sen. Maria Cantwell
for.role: Chair, Senate Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation
for.what_they_did: Reported the bill to the full Senate without amendment on December 17, 2024.

sides.party_line_note: The bill was sponsored by a Democrat and cosponsored by two Senate Democrats and two Senate Republicans, and the Senate Commerce Committee reported it favorably without recorded opposition; no one is on record against it — it simply never reached a floor vote.

industries.note: The bill would have imposed mandatory testing and certification costs, squeezing out makers of the cheapest uncertified batteries, while certified battery makers stood to gain from a rule that penalized non-compliant competitors. It never passed, so no costs or competitive shakeout occurred.

industries.industry: E-bike and e-scooter makers and retailers
industries.note: A mandatory standard would have raised compliance costs and, in some cases, retail prices, but also would have reduced the fire risk that has drawn scrutiny to the whole product category. Inaction leaves both the costs and the reputational risk in place.
